source.title: Small Batch Sizes Improve Training of Low-Resource Neural MT

record.tranche_reason: Tests batch-size effects on held-out performance in low-resource neural machine translation, extending batch-size findings to a new task and data regime.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own held-out BLEU results for batch-size conditions, including longer training and vocabulary comparisons. It does not measure train-versus-test error, gradient sharpness, or random-label memorization. Batch sizes 100 and 250 did not reach BLEU significantly above zero and were omitted from the results table.
record.test_reason: The study extends V5 to low-resource Transformer translation: it varies batch size under matched 700- and 1,400-epoch budgets and measures held-out BLEU. It also tests vocabulary changes. It is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is accurate if the mechanism remains explicitly hypothetical: moderately small batches improve held-out low-resource NMT performance and training efficiency, with performance degrading below an optimum. The authors attribute this plausibly to gradient regularization, but do not measure sharpness or establish that mechanism.
record.recipe_differences: Tests batch size in low-resource Transformer NMT, with BLEU and other MT metrics, rather than the original large-batch image-classification and language-model settings. The paper also changes vocabulary conditions and extends some runs to 1,400 epochs.
record.method_sensitivity: Batch size changes test performance; results are reported for HSB-DE and DE-EN, SentencePiece sharing conditions and BPE, and 700 versus 1,400 epochs.
record.problems: The models are low-resource NMT systems, so the findings do not directly establish results for the image classifiers or language models named in V5. Batch sizes 100 and 250 failed to reach BLEU significantly above zero and are omitted from Table 2. The main batch-size comparisons are reported with 95% significance statements; detailed significance exceptions are given in the text. Train error and a train-test generalization gap are not measured.
record.rows_left_out: Rows for dev Xent, dev BLEU, chrF, and TER, plus dev/test chrF and TER, are omitted because the main held-out test BLEU rows are retained and the paper's claim concerns held-out performance. Table 2 reports those metrics separately; the paper also discusses rankings by training time but gives no numerical values in the supplied text.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label generalization comparisons.
Width sweeps, interpolation thresholds, and generalization beyond zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD and sensitivity to optimizer tuning.

Image classification and standalone language modeling; batch-dependent learning-rate scaling, warmup adjustment, normalization or regularization changes, and training to matched update counts or established convergence.
Effects of adding or removing dropout. Dropout remains fixed at 0.1.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, generalization gaps, and comparisons with other generalization measures.
Identification and removal of memorized training examples.

missing.what: Batch sizes 100 and 250 did not achieve BLEU significantly above zero. Add the failed small-batch conditions with qualitative values; they establish the lower boundary of the useful batch-size range. Exact scores are not supplied.

record.verdict_notes: The record incorrectly says there is no matched fixed-epoch comparison: Section 5 explicitly holds training at 700 epochs, then at 1,400 for selected batches. Batch sizes are token counts; effective batches are four times the reported parameter. Adam, Noam scheduling and 8,000 warmup steps are fixed across conditions, so learning-rate schedules are not adapted to batch size. Translation is a new task setting for V5. The persistent gap after doubling epochs supports the fixed-budget result; it does not challenge V5's qualified statement that longer training can shrink or remove penalties. No training-error gap or sharpness is measured.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence; random-label held-out performance.
Width sweeps beyond interpolation and test error as a function of width.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD or momentum SGD and their held-out performance.

No image classifiers or language models outside low-resource NMT; no comparison of large batches with the smaller batch sizes under a matched, fixed epoch budget across a workload-dependent threshold. The paper compares batch sizes in low-resource NMT, reports 700-epoch and 1,400-epoch outcomes, and tests vocabulary variants.
Dropout intervention and its interaction with training-set size, data augmentation, and weight decay.
Magnitude-aware sharpness measurement and its relationship to the train-test gap.
Removing memorized examples and measuring held-out accuracy.
